title: Reading "large card count"
reading_goal: I understand that when the number of cards exceeds 1,000, attention must be paid to screen rendering and search performance.
question: What should you do when you have a lot of cards?
choices: It displays the content in sections so that it isn't rendered all at once.
answer: It displays the content in sections so that it isn't rendered all at once.
explanation: Card count alone does not determine when pagination is needed. One thousand is only an example threshold; measure card complexity, DOM nodes, device capability, and interaction latency before choosing pagination or virtualization. Separate full-data memory cost from DOM rendering cost.
project_context: Since the number of cards has exceeded 1,000, performance in bulk card loading, searching, and rendering—as well as user feedback—is now critical.

title: Reading About Pagination
reading_goal: Understand the concept of pagination, which displays a large number of cards in pages.
question: What is the purpose of pagination?
choices: To display a large number of items on a per-page basis,
answer: To display a large number of items on a per-page basis,
explanation: With a zero-based page, slice returns up to 50 items from page*50. Bound page to valid values and preserve total, previous and next state, and filters in URL or state. Pagination reduces visible DOM work but does not automatically reduce fetching all data.
project_context: Since the number of cards has exceeded 1,000, performance in bulk card loading, searching, and rendering—as well as user feedback—is now critical.

title: Read about lazy loading
reading_goal: Understand lazy loading, which loads data only when needed.
question: What are the advantages of lazy loading?
choices: You can quickly open the initial screen and load only the necessary data later.
answer: You can quickly open the initial screen and load only the necessary data later.
explanation: Loading review cards only when the tab opens defers initial network and parsing work. Coalesce repeated clicks and design loading, error, retry, cancellation, and prefetch behavior. Lazy loading moves the cost to another point in the user flow; it does not erase it.
project_context: Since the number of cards has exceeded 1,000, performance in bulk card loading, searching, and rendering—as well as user feedback—is now critical.

title: Reading the loading indicator
reading_goal: Understand the UI that displays the status to the user while data is being loaded.
question: Why is a loading indicator needed?
choices: To let you know that the app isn't frozen but is currently processing
answer: To let you know that the app isn't frozen but is currently processing
explanation: A loading indicator communicates pending work. finally hides it even on failure, while separate error and retry UI prevents an endless-loading impression. Expose busy state and status announcements to screen readers too.

title: Reading the empty state
reading_goal: Understand the "empty state," which displays a message when there are no search or filter results.
question: What is the role of the "empty state"?
choices: Clearly informs the user when there are no results
answer: Clearly informs the user when there are no results
explanation: An "empty state" is a screen displayed when there are no search results or data to show. If nothing is displayed, it can be difficult to tell whether there is an error or simply no results. A well-designed empty state guides the user on what to do next, reducing the feeling of being stuck. Therefore, the correct answer is “clearly inform the user when there are no results.”

title: Read about search debounce
reading_goal: Understand debouncing, which involves waiting a moment before executing a search query rather than executing it immediately upon each keystroke.
question: Why use debounce?
choices: To minimize unnecessary repetitive processing by running the search after the user has finished typing,
answer: To minimize unnecessary repetitive processing by running the search after the user has finished typing,
explanation: Canceling the timer delays search until 250 ms after the last input, reducing repeated filtering or requests. It does not cancel an already-started asynchronous search; use AbortController or a request sequence so old results cannot overwrite the latest query.
project_context: Since the number of cards has exceeded 1,000, performance in bulk card loading, searching, and rendering—as well as user feedback—is now critical.

title: Read about filtering performance
reading_goal: Understand the method of preparing search text in advance to improve filtering performance.
question: Why do we create the searchText for searching in advance?
choices: To avoid having to repeat the same string combinations every time I search,
answer: To avoid having to repeat the same string combinations every time I search,
explanation: Precomputing lowercased title and concept text avoids joining and lowercasing on every query. Rebuild the index when fields change and define locale and Unicode normalization. Apply it only when profiling justifies the extra memory and invalidation logic.

title: Reading the render cost
reading_goal: I understand that the more elements I create on the screen, the higher the rendering cost becomes.
question: What are some common situations where render costs increase?
choices: A situation where many card DOM elements are created at once
answer: A situation where many card DOM elements are created at once
explanation: Render cost refers to the processing overhead the browser incurs when drawing elements on the screen. If all cards—including those that are not visible—are added to the DOM, the rendering load increases. When there are many cards, it is necessary to use techniques such as pagination or virtual lists to reduce the number of elements that are actually rendered. Therefore, the correct answer is “a situation where a large number of cards are added to the DOM at once.”
project_context: Since the number of cards has exceeded 1,000, performance in bulk card loading, searching, and rendering—as well as user feedback—is now critical.

title: Reading a virtual list
reading_goal: Understand the concept of a virtual list, which renders only the visible items.
question: What is the key feature of a virtual list?
choices: Rendering only the items visible on the screen
answer: Rendering only the items visible on the screen
explanation: A virtual list keeps only viewport-adjacent rows in the DOM, reducing rendering and memory. It must handle dynamic heights, scroll position, keyboard focus, and screen-reader understanding of list position. Removing an offscreen focused node can break navigation.

title: Reading about incremental rendering
reading_goal: Understand incremental rendering, which renders a large list in multiple passes.
question: What is the purpose of incremental rendering?
choices: To break down large rendering tasks into smaller chunks and reduce screen freezes,
answer: To break down large rendering tasks into smaller chunks and reduce screen freezes,
explanation: Advance start and end and stop scheduling at the final card. Chunking gives the browser opportunities to paint, but an oversized chunk can still miss the frame budget. Also support cancellation and prevent duplicate runs.

title: Understanding `requestAnimationFrame`
reading_goal: Understand `requestAnimationFrame`, which schedules UI operations to align with the browser's rendering timing.
question: Why use `requestAnimationFrame`?
choices: To execute rendering operations in sync with the browser's screen refresh cycle,
answer: To execute rendering operations in sync with the browser's screen refresh cycle,
explanation: requestAnimationFrame schedules work before the next paint. A long renderVisibleCards callback still blocks the main thread and the frame, so reduce or chunk work or move pure calculation to a worker. Calls may be throttled in background tabs.

title: Reading Memory Usage

answer: Since browser memory usage can increase as the amount of data and screen elements grows,
explanation: Memory usage refers to the amount of memory occupied by card data, search indexes, and DOM elements. As the number of cards increases, you need to consider both the storage structure and screen rendering. If memory usage increases, the mobile browser may slow down or the tab may be forced to close.

title: Reading a Large JSON Split
reading_goal: Understand the strategy of splitting large datasets into multiple JSON files for loading.
code:
const neededFiles = selectLessonFiles(route, filters);
const lessons = await Promise.all(neededFiles.map(loadJson));
question: What are the advantages of splitting large JSON files?
choices: You can split the data into multiple files for management and load it in the units you need.
answer: You can split the data into multiple files for management and load it in the units you need.
explanation: Splitting data supports separate versions, caches, and selective loading. Promise.all over every lesson file still transfers all of them at once and can create connection and memory bursts. Select only needed files and define concurrency and error behavior.

explanation: A performance budget gives numerical regression targets for load, search, and rendering. These values are examples; specify device and network conditions, start and end points, and percentiles such as p75 or p95. When exceeded, profile the cause before changing product behavior.

title: Reading "Performance Measurement"
reading_goal: Understand the method of verifying performance based on measured values rather than subjective impressions.
question: Why use `console.time`?

answer: To measure how long a specific task takes,
explanation: console.time and timeEnd provide a quick elapsed-time measurement. One DevTools run can be skewed by JIT warmup, cache, and background work. Use Performance APIs, repeated benchmarks, and real-device percentiles for representative results.

title: Read "Large Card UX Strategy"
reading_goal: Understand strategies for designing loading, search, rendering, and feedback together in a card-based learning app.
question: What is the key to the "large card" UX strategy?
choices: Load quickly, display status, reduce search time, and render only what is visible
answer: Load quickly, display status, reduce search time, and render only what is visible
explanation: Fast first content, explicit loading and error states, debounce, and visible-only rendering are candidate strategies for large lists. Choose pagination, indexing, or virtualization from measured bottlenecks and user tasks rather than applying everything. Do not trade away search correctness or accessibility.
